features.auditNote: The jan-agent-harness crate (src-tauri/harness) was added by 7c48d71aa on the feat/agent-harness-phase-1 line and never reached the main line: merge 5534adb8e recorded that branch as incorporated with the integration tree kept, so its commits are ancestors of main but the crate is absent from main. A search of the tree found none of its types (HarnessEvent, EventPayload, ToolOutcome) under another name, so the code was lost, not moved. The original is recoverable from `git show 7c48d71aa:src-tauri/harness/src/event.rs` if it is to be restored. Update: AH-005 now provides a persisted versioned envelope (event_log.rs); tool phases and the renderer's run lifecycle are written to it, but the Rust loop's StreamEvents, steering and compaction are not, so it is not yet the sole source for streaming, journalling, audit and replay. 2026-09-11 (feat/integrated-phase-2): the Rust agent loop (CLI and the desktop's own agent runs) now writes to the session's canonical log: CompositeToolInvoker records every asked-for call before any gate and how it ended (succeeded, failed, or a typed refused with its kind), with input, output and its diff, under the run's session, run and agent (source agent-loop); orchestrate_inner records run.started and run.ended. Real CLI evidence: `jan cli agent run` against vLLM v100:8555 (pxa-27b) with an isolated JAN_DATA_FOLDER wrote run.started, tool.requested ls, tool.succeeded ls (output ".jan/ README.md"), run.ended to events/<session>.jsonl and nothing to the legacy file. Unit: the_loops_calls_are_recorded_in_the_session_log. Still in progress: the loop's streaming (text deltas, reasoning) and its steering and compaction are not written to the log, so it is not yet the sole source for streaming and replay. 2026-09-12 (Phase 3): one invocation id per provider request, everywhere. The Rust loop mints it (Invocations) and shares it with the tool invoker, so a CLI run records run.started, the dispatch with its prompt snapshot id, usage.reported, the reply, its tool calls under the same invocation, and run.ended (done/error) -- proven by a real `jan cli agent run` against the local model fixture, 10 events in order. Chat now writes the same contract as Cowork: a turn is one run even though Chat runs tools between requests (a reply asking for tools leaves the turn open), with usage and message events per request and tool events carrying the run and invocation instead of an empty run -- proven by the chat-execution-record WebView scenario (11 events, one run, invocation join, no leak into another session). Call folding is keyed by session + invocation + call so a reused provider call id is two calls, in the backend and on the Timeline. Still open: the CLI loop records no steering, compaction, reasoning or subagent lifecycle events; retention (32 MB per session, 500 sessions) has no test; and the 8555/8080 lanes were unavailable for this batch because the v100 host stopped resolving. 2026-09-12 (Phase 4): the rest of what a run does is in the same log. Per request: message.started when the reply first produces something (content or reasoning, whichever came first), message.reasoning with the size the provider supplied, beside the existing dispatch, usage and completion. Between requests, filed under the request last in flight: steering.received, compaction.started and its succeeded/failed outcome with the sizes, and agent.dispatched/agent.ended for a child the model started and awaited or cancelled. Sizes and counts only -- a stream-watcher forwards every event unchanged and writes none of the words. Retention now has direct tests: a full log keeps what it has, writes one log.truncated line and refuses the rest while staying valid JSONL across a restart; the oldest session logs go first and the one being written is never removed; a log from an older build reads back and the sequence continues into it. Real evidence: a CLI run against the reasoning fixture (message.started first=reasoning, message.reasoning chars=20 matching exactly what was streamed) and a seven-turn CLI session against an overflow fixture (compaction.started at 12 messages, the summarizer request, compaction.succeeded 12->10, then the retried dispatch and the reply). Still in progress: replay does not yet read this log (AH-032), so it is not the sole source for everything the criterion names; steering is TUI-only and is proven by loop and TUI tests rather than a WebView scenario. Later the same day: replay now reads this log (AH-032) for Cowork, Chat, the CLI and the desktop agent, which was the last thing standing between the record and the criterion. Read plainly, the criterion is about what is *persisted*: one versioned envelope is the only durable store the harness writes, and journalling, audit, export and replay all read it. Live streaming to a surface remains a transport (StreamEvent), and the record holds what streamed rather than being the channel it streamed through -- a log cannot be the wire. Moved to implemented on that reading; nothing else from the criterion is outstanding.

features.auditNote: Rebuilt on current interfaces (not restored from the lost src-tauri/harness crate, see 16ae36728): event_log.rs in the agent-tools plugin. One append-only JSON-lines log per session under <data>/events/. Envelope {v, id, session, run, invocation, seq, at, kind, payload, redactions}: v=1 and a newer version is a typed UnsupportedVersion; an unknown kind is kept and read back verbatim; ids are stable and a repeated id is one event (also after a restart); seq is assigned by the backend and strictly increasing per session; payloads are redacted with the plugin's redactor before writing and bounded to 64 KiB. A torn last line is skipped by readers and cut off before the next append; any other bad line is a typed Corrupt, never a silent gap. Each session log is bounded at 32 MiB (TooLarge) and the oldest of more than 500 logs are pruned. Writers: every tool phase through tool_activity_record, and run.started/run.ended/agent.dispatched/job.started/job.ended from the renderer through agent_events_record. Windows: event-export-1/2 read the log back through an export with an independent reader, in the durable tool-activity order, with the same ids after a real restart. Mutation-checked (dedup, torn-tail repair, version refusal, redaction). The Rust CLI/subagent loop's StreamEvents, steering and compaction are not yet written to it, which is why AH-004 remains in progress. macOS and Linux not run. Integration 2026-09-11 (feat/integrate-all-agent-workstreams): this log is now the only store of the execution record. activity::record writes each tool or lifecycle transition as one envelope (kind tool.<phase> / lifecycle.<phase>, id tool:<call>:<phase> / life:<call>:<phase>, payload = the redacted v2 activity event); tool_activity_record and the restart settlement both write through it, and the timeline, Background Tasks panel and audit_export are a projection folded from it. The pre-integration audit/tool-activity.jsonl is read for compatibility only (a transition in both stores counts once). Chat compaction and trim now reach the log as lifecycle events; the Rust CLI/subagent loop still writes nothing, so AH-004 stays in progress.

What was missing in behaviour was fixed instead, and two real defects were found doing it. (1) A --resume CLI run minted a fresh uuid session id, so seven turns of one conversation produced seven unrelated event logs, seven prompt histories and seven sets of changes; the session is now the thread, proven by a real seven-process run that produces one log, one session and seven distinct run ids (before: seven sessions, every run called #run-1). (2) A run id was a process counter, so the first run after a restart took the first run's id -- and since the record treats a repeated event id as one event, that run's start and end would be dropped and its work read as the earlier run's; ids now carry a base36 time part and sort by when they were minted. (3) A child run kept the parent's session but had no link to the parent run; it now records parentRun and the dispatch it answers, matching the parent's agent.dispatched, proven by a real CLI run that dispatches the shipped implementer role. Left in progress: there is no single identity type constructed and validated at a parsing boundary (ids are checked by the record's own input rules), and the resumed-conversation join has no desktop scenario yet. 2026-09-12 (Phase 5): the parsing boundary exists. identity gives session, run, invocation, job, agent and snapshot ids validated types -- bounded, no control characters, no path separator, no .., refused with a typed error rather than sanitised -- and the two storage boundaries (the event log and the durable job record) parse before they write, which matters because the session id names the file. Parentage is checked: a child must name a parent of the same session and nothing may be its own parent; a session id that is a prefix of another is not that session. A legacy id that would be refused today reads as nothing rather than as a value to store under, so old records stay readable without being trusted for policy. Desktop evidence: the identity-boundary scenario drives the renderer's own commands with five hostile spellings of a real session id and shows that none stores anything, none reads the real record, a near-miss id is a different empty session, and a run tree asked for with a hostile id is refused. Moved to implemented.

The original is recoverable from `git show 7c48d71aa:src-tauri/harness/src/error.rs` if it is to be restored. Per-module error kinds exist (ExportErrorKind, ChildErrorKind, ReplayErrorKind) but no shared taxonomy. 2026-09-12 (Phase 3): the taxonomy is restored from 7c48d71aa into the tools plugin (harness_error.rs) -- kind, retryability and audience on the value, with the model-facing "ERROR [tag]:" shape unchanged -- and given a classifier for provider failures. It is wired into two production paths: the provider chain reads may_try_another_provider for its fail-over decision (AH-193), and the headless CLI reads the classification to print [stopped] for a cancellation and [error:<kind>] otherwise, proven in a real run with no provider listening ([error:transport]). Left in progress deliberately: the orchestration loop still returns Result<_, String> internally and the per-module kinds (ExportErrorKind, ChildErrorKind, ReplayErrorKind) are not converted, so the single enum does not yet classify every harness failure. 2026-09-12 (Phase 4): the orchestration loop now speaks the taxonomy. ModelInvoker, ToolInvoker, run_turn_cycle, orchestrate_inner, compaction, the goal evaluator, the TUI compaction path and the headless CLI run all carry HarnessError instead of String. 26 kinds cover what the harness can fail at, including authentication apart from a permission refusal, rate limiting with the provider's own retry-after, context overflow, invalid response, sandbox denial, approval refusal, tool unavailable, tool failure, child failure, export, replay, interruption and malformed legacy state. Each error carries its stage and its cause; the serialized form is versioned, refusing a newer version and keeping a newer kind readable. Credentials are scrubbed when the error is built, not when it is shown -- proven end to end by a real CLI run against a provider that echoes the Authorization header back, where the key does not appear in the output. Every production decision now reads the kind: compaction retry, the AH-193 provider chain, the TUI's history reuse, the streamed error line, and the CLI exit status (sysexits: 77 for a rejected credential, 69 for a provider that was not there, 130 for a stop) -- both proven by real runs. Adversarial tests show misleading wording cannot move the fallback decision either way. Still in progress: the tool layer still returns refusals as ERROR-prefixed strings in tool results, and the desktop's ExportErrorKind/ChildErrorKind/ReplayErrorKind are not yet folded into this enum. 2026-09-12 (Phase 5): the last two boundaries are typed. The tool layer keeps its text interface to the model -- that is the protocol -- but nothing decides anything by reading it any more: classify_tool turns a result into a classification once (a handler's own ERROR [kind]: tag taken at its word, the built-in shapes read otherwise, anything unrecognised a tool_failed that is never retried on that basis), and the tool boundary, the transcript flag and the activity record all read that one answer. The record carries error_kind beside the phase, and a cancelled or timed-out call is recorded as such rather than as a failure. The parallel enums (event export, bundle import, child checkouts, worktree export, replay) cross by explicit From written case by case, so a link escape is a policy violation and not an I/O fault. Real evidence: a CLI run whose three failing calls are recorded as tool_failed, invalid_input and tool_unavailable -- the third being a defect this evidence found and fixed. Moved to implemented.

features.auditNote: The ceiling now stops the run. Crossing it used to record a system note and carry on, tool calls included, which -- with max_turns == 0 the normal case -- left user cancellation as the only bound on a run's spend: a run that went wrong could spend without limit while announcing that it had passed its limit. run_turn_cycle now returns as soon as the budget is exhausted. The turn that crossed the line is finished and returned intact, so its text and its tool_calls are preserved in the transcript; what stops is the next thing -- the tool calls that turn asked for are not dispatched and no further turn is taken. The system note says how many calls were skipped. features.auditNote: Every built-in now runs under a deadline, not just bash. lifecycle::Timeouts gives a default plus per-tool limits and overrides, and an unknown tool gets the default rather than no limit. execute_builtin wraps the handler in run_with_deadline, so the clock starts when execution starts -- after the gate, not while a call waited for approval -- and a stopped call reports whether it hit a deadline or a person. The bash timeout previously *backgrounded* the command: it kept running, unowned, after the call returned, so the deadline and the stop were unrelated events. It now terminates the process tree, preserves whatever the command printed first, and warns rather than claiming success if the tree did not die; backgrounding survives as an explicit background:true argument. CORRECTION to the prior audit note: MCP tool calls already had both a timeout and a cancellation channel (core/mcp/commands.rs:494-506, tool_call_timeout_duration); the claim that they had none was wrong. features.auditNote: The snapshot is taken in HttpModelInvoker::invoke from `normalized` -- the exact serialized request, after context construction and after the model id is rewritten, at the last point before dispatch. Not reconstructed from earlier state. It carries schema version, stable id, RFC3339 UTC timestamp, session, run, thread, agent, provider, model, reasoning configuration, the redacted payload, its hash, and the redaction list; message count, tool names and system prompt are derived from the payload rather than stored twice. Redaction runs while the record is built, walks the whole document (a credential in a nested tool argument leaks as surely as one in a header), matches credential fields by name because an auth header's value is opaque, and still applies the value-shaped pass to free text for an env line pasted into a prompt. Each removal records its path and reason, so an empty field is distinguishable from a redacted one. The hash is FNV-1a over a canonical key-sorted serialization of the *redacted* payload: identical payloads hash identically however built, any change to a retry produces a different hash, and a reader can verify the record against its own hash. Storage is append-only JSONL at <jan_data>/audit/prompts.jsonl, flushed per record, with a reader that drops an unparseable line so a truncated tail costs one record. Lookup by id, run and session. A snapshot that cannot be taken is recorded as explicitly unavailable with its reason and identity intact. StreamEvent::PromptSnapshot carries id, hash and redaction count to the activity timeline, never the payload. Guards mutation-checked: removing redaction, and making the hash ignore its input, each turn the relevant tests red. The viewer is built (PromptSnapshotView, verified by cowork-smoke --only prompt-snapshot-panel), and a snapshot is now bound to the assistant turn that produced it rather than matched by position. Six earlier designs wrote the reference from the snapshot sink onto 'the last assistant turn'; instrumenting the live turn lane in the running app showed the lane holds only the user turn at dispatch time, so there was no assistant row to write onto and every one of those writes silently did nothing -- while passing in vitest, which hands the mutation an array that already contains one. The attach happens in pushLive, where the row is created, from the dispatch that just went out; coworkTurns.ts already emitted a data-prompt-snapshot part for any turn carrying one, so nothing downstream needed changing. The render prefers the message's own part and keeps positional matching as a fallback for turns written to disk before rows carried one. Proven by mutation in the real WebView: with the positional fallback disabled entirely the panel still renders, so the per-turn reference is what carries it. A continuation, a retry and a compaction each carry their own snapshot, which is what position could not express. 2026-09-11: retention and deletion added -- the log keeps the newest 2000 snapshots (checked when it passes 8 MB), deleting a Chat thread or Cowork session deletes its snapshots (agent_prompt_snapshots_delete), both by an atomic temp-and-rename rewrite that keeps unattributable torn lines. Stored as credential-redacted plaintext like conversation history; not encrypted. Snapshot ids now carry the process launch (snap-<launch>-<n>): the plain counter restarted at snap-1 in every launch, so an id could name an earlier launch's record in the same log.
features.evidence: Captured in core/net/transport.rs::capture_snapshot, at the last point before a provider request leaves the process -- the one path every OpenAI-compatible request takes -- from the exact serialized body that is dispatched. Redacted before it is written; FNV-1a hash over the canonical key-sorted redacted payload; append-only JSONL at <jan_data>/audit/prompts.jsonl. Retrieval is scoped: an id alone is refused, and an unscoped list is refused (agent_prompt_snapshots -> snapshot::scoped_lookup). The reference reaches the timeline through the transport's head chunk and a session-keyed store, and the Nth dispatch renders under the Nth assistant message, so a snapshot sits with its own invocation. Smoke: prompt-snapshot-panel (performs a real model request over http://v100:8080/v1, asserts the dispatch was recorded on disk, opens the panel, checks provider/model/session/hash/redactions, switches tree and JSON views, and asserts no credential appears) and prompt-snapshot-cross-session-refused (a snapshot id with another session's scope returns nothing; an unscoped list errors).

features.auditNote: A stored prompt snapshot is sent to the model again from its panel ('Replay this context'). The backend (core/agent/replay.rs) looks the snapshot up within its session and hands out the stored payload; the renderer never assembles it. Refusals are typed and recorded: not-found (including another session's id, which leaves no record), unavailable, redacted (a snapshot with any redaction is not the whole context), not-a-chat, and, on the renderer side, provider-gone, provider-unsupported (Anthropic wire format, MLX) and model-not-running (a local model is never started for a replay). The request goes through the ordinary provider transport under agent 'replay' (ignored by the timeline sink); settle compares the transport's snapshot of that dispatch with the original by hash, scoped to the session, so 'matched' is checked on the record. Tool calls in the reply are recorded by name and never executed. Endings: completed, failed (provider-error, stream-cut-off), cancelled (AbortController stops the transport stream), refused; first ending kept; a running record from an earlier process reads as interrupted; one the current window no longer holds is recorded as abandoned. Records are redacted and bounded before they are written to <data>/replays. Found and fixed on the way: snapshot ids restarted at snap-1 in every launch, so an id could name an earlier launch's record. The copy carries the tail only (40 messages, 96 KB) and says so when that bound really cut; it leaves behind the parent's system prompt, orphan tool results, and the unanswered dispatch call itself, because a provider rejects either half of a tool exchange. features.auditNote: Reclassified from implemented (2026-09-11). Spawn-without-blocking and await-later work (dispatch_subagent / await_subagent; the Cowork task tool), but the persistence criterion is not met: children are run-scoped futures, aborted on parent teardown (AbortOnDrop) and gone at app exit. After a restart the record is truthful -- the desktop marks unfinished children interrupted by application exit -- but nothing survives or resumes. Meeting it needs a durable worker outside the app process, which does not exist. 2026-09-12 (Phase 4): the durable half exists. Every background job is written down under <data>/jobs/ (keyed by a hash of the owner, so a conversation id is never a path component) with its owner, the run and invocation that started it, a redacted bounded command summary and how it ended. Identity is the pid *and* the process creation time, so a reused pid can never be mistaken for ours: a restart marks a job whose process is gone interrupted (an ending nobody saw is never a completion), one whose pid now belongs to something else orphaned and untouched, and one that cannot be identified interrupted -- dropping the pid in every case so nothing acts on it later. Proven by a real WebView pair across an actual restart plus three unit tests. Still in progress, and this is the whole remaining criterion: the work itself does not survive the app, because a job is the app's child process and a subagent is a future inside it. The CLI binary already runs the same loop headlessly, so the shape of a durable worker exists, but nothing spawns one or re-attaches to it. 2026-09-12 (Phase 5): the work itself now survives. A job is run by a detached supervisor process (jan cli job supervise, the CLI binary that ships beside the app), so the starting process can exit and the work continues; the supervisor writes the output as it is produced and the ending when it comes, which is what makes a completion knowable rather than merely "its process is gone". features.auditNote: Implemented 2026-09-13 (Phase 5). `jan cli agent licenses [--allow ...] [--record] [--json]` reads cargo crates via `cargo metadata --offline` and npm packages from each installed package.json (the deprecated licenses array included), and judges each declared licence against [licenses].allow. Only declared identifiers are used -- matching by licence text is how a project comes to believe a modified MIT is MIT -- and a dependency that declares nothing is listed as declaring nothing, never as allowed. `OR` needs either, `AND` needs both, a parenthesised expression is reported rather than judged by halves, and "*" allows anything declared without ever making an undeclared licence declared. A disallowed dependency exits policy_violation. features.auditNote: 2026-09-12 (Phase 3): implemented in the agent loop. `[agent].fallback` in agent.toml is an ordered, opt-in chain; each entry resolves like the primary model and an unresolvable one is logged and skipped rather than failing the run. Only failures that say the request never reached a model are failed over (connection refused, DNS, 502/503/504, timeout); anything a provider answered -- 401/403, an invalid key, a context-length refusal, a 400, a cancelled run -- is not, which is also what makes the guarantees hold: a dispatch that never reached a model produced no output, ran no tool and took no approval, so nothing can be duplicated. Every attempt is its own invocation, the fallback is recorded (phase fell-back, from, to, reason, the request it follows) and the usage is attributed to the provider that answered (answeredBy). Real evidence: a two-lane CLI run (dead primary port, local fixture backup) answered from the backup with the whole chain in the record, and the same run against a 401 fixture failed without falling back. Limit: the chain is agent.toml configuration, so Chat and Cowork -- which have no chain UI -- never fail over, and compaction/goal-evaluation dispatches keep their own provider. 2026-09-12 (Phase 4): hardened without reopening. The chain is now the providers that have not been tried yet: the primary and any repeat (in any case, with blanks dropped) are removed before the first attempt, because trying a provider that has already failed cannot help and doubles what the user waits for. Every decision reads the AH-009 classification rather than the wording, and the ten failure shapes the phase set out to be sure of are covered by a test: connection failure, timeout, rate limit and an unavailable gateway earn the next provider; authentication, a refusal, a context overflow, an unsupported capability, a malformed stream and a cancellation do not. The malformed stream is the one that matters most -- part of the reply may already be on screen, so retrying it elsewhere could duplicate output. Real evidence: a three-lane CLI run where two lanes are not listening and the third answers, with the repeat and the primary skipped, each attempt under its own invocation, and the answer attributed to the provider that produced it.

features.auditNote: forkSession copies the conversation up to a named turn and records parent and divergence. features.title: Provider cache-aware token accounting
acceptanceCriteria: Provider-reported input, cached input, cache write, output and total tokens are normalized from the wire formats Jan uses (OpenAI-compatible prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens, Anthropic cache_read/cache_creation_input_tokens, llama.cpp usage and timings.cache_n, and other providers only where their converter reports cache counts), with uncached input derived as max(input - cached, 0).
A count the provider did not report stays unknown end to end and is never displayed or stored as zero; a measured zero is displayed as zero.

Cache-creation tokens are part of the input total and of its uncached share and are never counted twice; inconsistent provider values are clamped and the reported values retained; cumulative streaming usage keeps the final values rather than summing snapshots.

The breakdown survives the Chat and Cowork paths -- converters, streaming metadata, the transport callback, Chat message persistence, Cowork runner events, session persistence and subagent usage -- and an application restart; records saved before it existed load unchanged and read as not reported.

The Chat and Cowork token counter keeps its compact badge and shows Input, Cached input, Uncached input, Cache write (when reported), Output and Total in its popover, with an explanation that uncached input is derived and is a token count, not a count of cache misses.
Provider-reported usage stays separate from AH-073's dispatched-payload estimate, which is never presented as provider usage.
Tests: unit, provider-parsing and real WebView coverage, including a real provider that reports cache counts and a restart.
